passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of caffeine on working memory performance in a controlled laboratory setting. Twenty-eight healthy adults (age 20-35) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: (1) placebo, (2) low-dose caffeine (50 mg), (3) moderate-dose caffeine (100 mg), and (4) high-dose caffeine (200 mg). Each participant completed a 2‑back task after ingesting their assigned beverage. Reaction times (RT) and accuracy were recorded. The researchers hypothesized that moderate caffeine would yield the fastest RTs and highest accuracy, with performance declining at the high dose due to overstimulation. Table 1 presents the mean RTs and standard deviations for each group. The study also measured subjective alertness using a 10‑point Likert scale. Results indicated a U‑shaped relationship between caffeine dose and RT, supporting the hypothesis. However, accuracy did not vary significantly across groups, suggesting caffeine primarily affected speed rather than correctness.
stem: Which group had the fastest mean reaction time?
explanation: The moderate‑dose group (100 mg) had the lowest mean RT of 520 ms, the fastest among all groups.
trap: Assuming the largest dose must give the fastest responses and picking the high-dose group (580 ms), when the moderate dose had the lowest RT (520 ms).

stem: Which feature of the study design best controls for the effect of participants' expectations about receiving a stimulant?

options.B: Measuring accuracy as well as RT
options.D: Using a 10-point Likert scale for alertness

explanation: Correct: a placebo beverage gives all participants the same expectation, so effects of caffeine can be separated from expectation. Why the others are wrong: B) Accuracy is another outcome, not a control. C) An age range restricts the sample but does not control expectancy. D) A rating scale measures alertness only.
trap: Picking the age restriction or the alertness scale because they sound like controls; only a placebo gives every participant the same expectation of receiving a stimulant.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: RTs follow a U‑shaped curve across doses
options.B: Accuracy did not vary significantly across groups

explanation: Correct: the high-dose group (580 ms) was slower than the moderate-dose group (520 ms). Why the others are wrong: A) 650, 590, 520, 580 ms is U-shaped. B) The passage states this. C) 520 ms is the lowest.
trap: Assuming more caffeine means faster responses.

stem: Which psychological principle is most directly illustrated by the study’s findings?
explanation: The Yerkes-Dodson law predicts optimal performance at moderate arousal, with poorer performance at low and high arousal, matching the best RT at 100 mg and slower RTs at 50 and 200 mg.
trap: Choosing the law of diminishing returns because gains seem to shrink at high dose; here performance actually worsened at 200 mg, matching an inverted-U arousal-performance relation.
